chapters.title: Chapter 1. Mr. Sherlock Holmes
chapters.synopsis: At 221B Baker Street, Sherlock Holmes asks Dr. Watson to deduce the character of a visitor from a walking stick left behind the night before. Watson's guesses are partly wrong, and Holmes corrects them: the stick, engraved from the C.C.H., suggests Charing Cross Hospital, and its owner is a young, amiable, absent-minded country doctor with a spaniel. Watson confirms the man's career in the Medical Directory. Dr. James Mortimer of Grimpen, Dartmoor then arrives, retrieves his stick, admires Holmes's skull, and is rebuked for naming Bertillon as the foremost expert. Holmes asks him to state the problem plainly.

chapters.title: Chapter 2. The Curse of the Baskervilles
chapters.synopsis: In the sitting room at Baker Street, Dr. Mortimer reads Holmes and Watson an 1742 family manuscript telling how Hugo Baskerville abducted a yeoman's daughter, hunted her across the moor, and was killed by a gigantic black hound, which allegedly plagues the family. Holmes dismisses it as a fairy tale until Mortimer reads a Devon County Chronicle account of the recent death of Sir Charles Baskerville, found dead in the yew alley of Baskerville Hall, with the inquest finding natural heart failure. Mortimer then privately reveals that Sir Charles feared the legend, that he saw a black calf-like creature weeks earlier, and that Mortimer found footprints near the body that he concealed from the inquest. He ends by announcing they were the footprints of a gigantic hound.

chapters.title: Chapter 3. The Problem
chapters.synopsis: In Holmes's Baker Street rooms, Dr. Mortimer finishes describing the footprints of a gigantic hound near Sir Charles's body, then answers Holmes's questions about the yew alley, the wicket-gate and the cigar ash. He admits he half-believes in a supernatural cause because several people saw a spectral creature on the moor before the death. He asks Holmes's advice about Sir Henry Baskerville, the heir arriving at Waterloo Station within the hour. Holmes tells him to meet Sir Henry, say nothing, and bring him to Baker Street at ten the next morning. Holmes spends the day smoking over an Ordnance map, and Watson returns that evening to hear him lay out the geography and reason that Sir Charles was running in terror and was waiting for someone at the moor-gate.

chapters.title: Chapter 4. Sir Henry Baskerville
chapters.synopsis: At ten o'clock Dr. Mortimer brings Sir Henry Baskerville to Baker Street. Sir Henry shows an anonymous warning letter, made of words pasted from a Times leading article, that reached him at the Northumberland Hotel, and mentions that one of his new boots has gone missing. Holmes analyses the letter, then hears Mortimer retell the legend, and Sir Henry firmly refuses to be kept from Baskerville Hall. After the visitors leave for their hotel, Holmes and Watson follow them down Oxford and Regent Streets and spot a bearded man in a hansom cab, who escapes. Holmes notes the cab number 2704 and sends the messenger boy Cartwright to search the Charing Cross hotels' waste-paper for the cut-up Times page.

chapters.title: Chapter 5. Three Broken Threads
chapters.synopsis: Holmes and Watson return to the Northumberland Hotel, where Holmes checks the register and learns the people interested in Sir Henry are not staying there. Sir Henry is furious over a second missing boot, an old black one, but the missing brown boot is later found under a cabinet in the sitting-room. Over luncheon Holmes learns of Sir Charles's will, in which Barrymore received five hundred pounds, Mortimer a thousand, and Sir Henry the residue of about seven hundred forty thousand pounds, with James Desmond next in line. Holmes tests whether Barrymore, who has a black beard, is in London by telegram, and asks Watson to accompany Sir Henry to Devon on Saturday's ten-thirty train from Paddington. That evening telegrams show Barrymore is at the Hall and Cartwright found no trace of the cut Times sheet. Cabman John Clayton then reveals his fare gave the name Sherlock Holmes, leaving Holmes checkmated in London and uneasy about sending Watson.

chapters.title: Chapter 6. Baskerville Hall
chapters.synopsis: Holmes sees Watson and Sir Henry off at the station, instructing Watson to report facts and keep watch on those around Sir Henry on the moor, while clearing the heir James Desmond of suspicion and keeping the Barrymores as suspects. The party travels to Devon by train, then by wagonette past armed soldiers hunting Selden, the Notting Hill murderer who has escaped from Princetown. They reach Baskerville Hall at dusk, where Barrymore greets them and says he and his wife wish to leave. After a gloomy dinner, Watson lies awake in his room and hears a woman sobbing somewhere in the house.

chapters.title: Chapter 7. The Stapletons of Merripit House
chapters.synopsis: The morning after arrival, Watson and Sir Henry discuss the woman's sobbing heard at night; Barrymore denies it was his wife, but Watson sees Mrs. Barrymore's red, swollen eyes and suspects he lied. Watson walks to Grimpen to check the test telegram and learns it was given to Mrs. Barrymore, not Barrymore himself, so Barrymore's presence in London is not disproved. On the way back, the naturalist Stapleton introduces himself, shows Watson the Grimpen Mire, a pony dying in it, and prehistoric huts, and they hear a eerie moaning he attributes to bogs or a bittern. At Merripit House Stapleton's sister Beryl urgently tells Watson to leave the moor, mistaking him for Sir Henry, then later claims it was a whim and that she only feared the family curse. Watson returns to the Hall with deeper suspicion.

chapters.title: Chapter 8. First Report of Dr. Watson
chapters.synopsis: Chapter 8 is Watson's first written report to Holmes from Baskerville Hall on October 13th. He describes the moor's prehistoric huts, the escaped convict who is thought to have fled, and Sir Henry's growing attraction to Miss Stapleton, which her brother seems to disapprove of. He recounts the excursion to the legend's stone site, the walk through the yew alley with Dr. Mortimer, and the litigious neighbour Mr. Frankland, who scans the moor with a telescope. Barrymore says his wife delivered and answered the test telegram. That night Watson follows Barrymore and sees him holding a candle at an empty room's window, staring at the moor, before he groans and extinguishes it.

chapters.title: Chapter 9. The Light upon the Moor [Second Report of Dr. Watson]
chapters.synopsis: At Baskerville Hall, Watson reports to Holmes. After finding that Barrymore's window has the closest view of the moor, Watson tells Sir Henry, who agrees to watch him. Sir Henry slips out to meet Miss Stapleton on the moor; Watson follows and sees Stapleton furiously interrupt Sir Henry's proposal. Stapleton later apologises and asks Sir Henry to wait three months, and they are to dine at Merripit House. On the second night's vigil they catch Barrymore signalling with a candle; Mrs. Barrymore reveals that she is born Selden and the convict is her brother, whom they are feeding. Watson and Sir Henry chase Selden on the moor, hear the hound-like cry, and see a tall, motionless stranger on a tor after losing the convict.

chapters.title: Chapter 10. Extract from the Diary of Dr. Watson
chapters.synopsis: On October 16th, a foggy day after the night chase, Watson broods over the hound, the human agency in London, and the stranger on the tor. Barrymore pleads that the police not be told Selden is still on the moor, promising he will soon leave for South America, and Sir Henry agrees. Barrymore also reveals that Sir Charles received a letter from Coombe Tracey signed L. L., asking him to burn it and be at the gate at ten o'clock. On October 17th, Watson walks the rainy moor and learns from Dr. Mortimer that Laura Lyons, Frankland's estranged daughter living in Coombe Tracey, has those initials. That evening Barrymore tells Watson that Selden has told him of another man hiding in the stone huts on the moor, served by a lad who brings supplies, and Watson resolves to reach the heart of the mystery.

chapters.title: Chapter 11. The Man on the Tor
chapters.synopsis: Watson, having learned that Laura Lyons wrote to Sir Charles and that the lurker is in the stone huts, drives to Coombe Tracey and questions Mrs. Lyons. She at first denies, then admits writing the letter asking Sir Charles to meet her at the gate at ten, but swears she never went because help came from another source, and Watson finds her story coherent yet suspects she hides something. On the way back he meets Mr. Frankland, who boasts of his lawsuits and reveals through his telescope that a boy carries food to the hidden man near Black Tor. Watson walks to the stony hill, finds the stranger's hut empty but lived in, and reads a note saying 'Dr. Watson has gone to Coombe Tracey', showing he is being watched. As he waits in the hut at dusk, footsteps approach and a well-known voice greets him.

chapters.title: Chapter 12. Death on the Moor
chapters.synopsis: In the dusk at the stone hut near Black Tor, Watson discovers that the voice was Holmes, who has secretly been living on the moor with Cartwright's help while Watson's reports were read by him. Holmes reveals that Miss Stapleton is really Stapleton's wife, that Stapleton is a former schoolmaster who is the enemy, and that Laura Lyons believed he would marry her. A terrible scream and the hound's rumble send them running, and they find a body in Sir Henry's clothes that is actually the convict Selden, who wore the baronet's cast-off wardrobe. Stapleton arrives, is shocked and disappointed, and probes what they heard; Holmes feigns that he is leaving for London. Walking back to the Hall, Holmes explains that they lack provable evidence and plans to use Laura Lyons and Sir Henry's dinner at the Stapletons'.

chapters.title: Chapter 13. Fixing the Nets
chapters.synopsis: At Baskerville Hall, Holmes tells Sir Henry of Selden's death and the Barrymores are informed; Mrs. Barrymore weeps for her brother. Holmes notices the portrait of the wicked Hugo Baskerville and sees Stapleton's face in it, concluding Stapleton is a Baskerville with designs on the succession. Next morning Holmes arranges that Sir Henry dine at Merripit House and walk home alone along the straight path, while Holmes and Watson feign leaving for London. At Coombe Tracey station Holmes sends Cartwright to London, receives Lestrade's telegram, and then confronts Laura Lyons with proof that Stapleton (the Vandeleurs of St. Oliver's school) is married. She admits Stapleton dictated her letter and kept her silent. Lestrade arrives, and Holmes proposes taking him to Dartmoor that night.

chapters.title: Chapter 14. The Hound of the Baskervilles
chapters.synopsis: Holmes, Watson and Lestrade return to the moor at night and hide in an ambush near Merripit House while Sir Henry dines with Stapleton. A fog creeping off Grimpen Mire threatens the plan, but Sir Henry walks out in time and a huge, luminous black hound bounds out of the fog after him. Holmes and Watson shoot the hound dead before it kills Sir Henry, and Watson identifies the glow as phosphorus. Stapleton has fled, and in the house they find Mrs. Stapleton bound and bruised in the museum room; she says he has fled to an old tin mine on an island in the mire. Next morning she guides them to the path, where Holmes finds Sir Henry's missing boot and concludes Stapleton is buried in the mire. On the island they find the hound's kennel, the skeleton of Mortimer's spaniel and the luminous paste, and Holmes explains the scheme.

chapters.title: Chapter 15. A Retrospection
chapters.synopsis: At the end of November, in the Baker Street sitting-room, Holmes and Watson discuss the Baskerville case after Sir Henry and Dr. Mortimer have called on their way to a long voyage. Holmes retraces the whole affair: Stapleton's true Baskerville parentage, his Vandeleur school past, his plan to inherit, the creation of the phosphorus hound, the death of Sir Charles, the London attempts on Sir Henry, and Holmes's secret work on the moor. He explains Mrs. Stapleton's role and why she turned on her husband, and admits he cannot say how Stapleton would have claimed the estate. He then proposes an evening at the opera and dinner at Marcini's.

mention.quote: Sherlock Holmes

summary.text: Sherlock Holmes is an investigator who reasons from physical clues, such as the marks on a stick, a cigarette stub marked Bradley, Oxford Street, and a scent suggesting a lady, and who insists that all other hypotheses be exhausted before the supernatural one is accepted. He is usually very late in the mornings unless he has been up all night, and he has written a monograph on dating documents. He takes on the matter of Sir Henry, whom he believes is being warned by someone not ill-disposed towards him, and he tells Mortimer to say nothing to Sir Henry until he has made up his mind. After declaring himself checkmated in London, he sends Watson to the moor, asking only for facts and keeping the theorizing for himself. The narrator reveals in chapter 12 that Holmes is the hidden stranger in the hut, having deliberately let Watson believe he was in Baker Street, and Holmes says he had been reading Watson's reports. Barrymore reports Selden's claim that the stranger had a lad bringing him supplies, and Watson believes an agent, perhaps the boy, was set on his track, but these are beliefs. Holmes says there is no provable case against Stapleton, that risks must be taken to establish one, and that he stayed mostly at Coombe Tracey, using the hut only when he needed to be near the scene of action.

He also confesses that once, when very young, he confused the Leeds Mercury with the Western Morning News, and he believes, by his own reasoning rather than established fact, that someone who warns Sir Henry of danger is not ill-disposed towards him.

personality.text: Sherlock Holmes is keenly observant, reading small details such as the tooth marks a dog left on a heavy stick (ch1). He is also rational, insisting that all other hypotheses be exhausted before a particular one is accepted (ch3). He is candid about his own mistakes, admitting that he once confused the Leeds Mercury with the Western Morning News when he was very young (ch4). He is controlling in his working relationships, asking that facts be reported to him fully and leaving the theorizing to himself (ch6). His voice is described as cold, incisive, and ironical (ch12), and he can be deceptive, as when he admits that he wished another person to believe something untrue (ch12).

personality.text: Watson is shown as a devoted admirer of Holmes, so much so that he is piqued when Holmes meets his admiration and his efforts to publicize Holmes's methods with indifference (ch 1). He is obliging by nature, readily agreeing to join Holmes with the words "I will come, with pleasure" (ch 5). He is also humane and restrained: though a lucky long shot from his revolver might have crippled the fleeing man, he had brought the weapon only for self-defense and would not shoot an unarmed man who was running away (ch 9). Alongside this he has a dryly pragmatic streak, remarking with a shrug that if a man were safely out of the country it would relieve the tax-payer of a burden (ch 10).

summary.text: Dr. James Mortimer, also addressed as Mister Mortimer, is a tall, thin man with a long beak-like nose, close-set keen grey eyes and gold-rimmed glasses, who practises at Grimpen on Dartmoor, Devon. Dr. Watson states that he was a house-surgeon at Charing Cross Hospital from 1882 to 1884, serves as medical officer for the parishes of Grimpen, Thorsley and High Barrow, and has published 'Some Freaks of Atavism' and 'Do We Progress?'; Mortimer himself says he left the hospital after his marriage and insists on being called Mister, as a humble M.R.C.S. He comes to Holmes with what he calls a serious and extraordinary problem, speaking as a trustee and executor of Sir Charles's will and as someone Sir Charles left a thousand pounds. By his own account, he found fresh footprints, which he says were those of a gigantic hound, some twenty yards from the body, and withheld them from the coroner's inquiry because a man of science shrinks from seeming to indorse a popular superstition. The narrator adds that he has a wife and a spaniel, that he has been excavating a barrow at Long Down and has obtained a prehistoric skull, and that the spaniel later disappeared on the moor.

summary.text: Sir Charles Baskerville is a widower of somewhat eccentric habit of mind who, according to the narrator, made large sums of money in South African speculation. Dr. James Mortimer states that nothing would induce him to go out upon the moor at night, yet he died there, lying on his face with arms outstretched, fingers dug into the ground, and features so convulsed that Mortimer could hardly have sworn to his identity. Mortimer also states that Sir Charles had evidently stood at the moor-gate for five or ten minutes, since the ash had twice dropped from his cigar, and the coroner's jury returned a verdict in accordance with the medical evidence. Sherlock Holmes believes Sir Charles ran desperately for his life until his heart burst, and thinks it unlikely that he waited at the gate every evening, given that he avoided the moor; Barrymore, by contrast, believes Sir Charles was at the gate to meet a woman. Holmes later states that Sir Charles fell dead at the end of the alley from heart disease and terror.

personality.text: Hugo Baskerville is characterized as a most wild, profane, and godless man (ch 2). His irreverence toward the sacred is shown plainly in his open disregard for religion (ch 2). He is also reckless and defiant, crying aloud before all the company that he would that very night render his body and soul to the Powers of Evil if he might but overtake the wench (ch 2). This willingness to stake his soul on a whim shows a man who flouts both moral and spiritual limits in front of others (ch 2).

summary.text: The Hound of the Baskervilles is a creature tied to a family legend, which describes a great black beast shaped like a hound, larger than any hound, that in a 17th-century flashback to the Time of the Great Rebellion stood over Hugo Baskerville on the moor, plucking at his throat. According to the legend, many members of the family have since met sudden, bloody, mysterious deaths because of it. Later chapters present a physical animal: it is a cross of bloodhound and mastiff, as large as a small lioness, and its fiery glow comes from phosphorus prepared so as to give off no smell that might disturb its scent. Watson and Holmes hear a deep, muttered, menacing rumble like the murmur of the sea, and Holmes believes the hound was set on Selden using Sir Henry's stolen boot. Holmes states that it kept to the grassy border while the baronet ran down the path, so that no track but the man's was visible, and he emptied five barrels of his revolver into its flank.

summary.text: Barrymore, also called John, is the full-bearded butler of Sir Charles at the Hall, the son of the old caretaker, from a family that Dr. James Mortimer says has looked after the Hall for four generations. On the night of Sir Charles's death he found the hall door open at twelve o'clock, became alarmed, and went searching for his master with a lantern. He later tells Holmes that he and his wife wish to leave, citing attachment to Sir Charles and his death, and saying Sir Charles's generosity gives them the means to start a business; Holmes nonetheless keeps the Barrymores on his list of suspects. Watson believes Barrymore lied and wonders whether he might be the bearded man seen in the cab in Regent Street, noting that the test telegram went to Mrs. Barrymore, so it is not proven that he was at the Hall rather than in London. Barrymore is then found crouching at a window in the night with a candle held against the glass, and Mrs. Barrymore explains that the light is a signal telling the convict that food is ready; Barrymore afterward assures Sir Henry that Selden will soon be on his way to South America, and swears that foul play and black villainy are brewing.

summary.text: Sir Henry Baskerville, the son of Sir Charles Baskerville's younger brother, is the heir to the Baskerville estate and, according to Dr. James Mortimer, the last of the Baskervilles. He is described as a small, alert, dark-eyed man of about thirty, sturdily built, with thick black eyebrows and a strong, pugnacious face. Having spent nearly all his time in the States and Canada, where he had been farming, he is unfamiliar with British life, and he says he was a boy in his teens when his father died, lived in a cottage on the South Coast, and had never seen the Hall. Although he says he has heard of the hound since his nursery days, he declares that no devil in hell and no man on earth can stop him from going to the home of his own people. At the Hall he becomes strongly attracted to Miss Stapleton, a feeling Watson believes was mutual, and he offers to marry her, though her brother interrupts before she can answer. Later events leave him insensible and then delirious with fever after a night's shock, and Holmes states that his love for the lady was deep and sincere and that the saddest part for him was having been deceived by her.

He is a small, alert, dark-eyed man of about thirty, sturdily built, with thick black eyebrows and a strong, pugnacious face. He spent nearly all his time in the States and Canada, where he had been farming, and is unfamiliar with British life; he was a boy in his teens when his father died, lived in a cottage on the South Coast, and had never seen the Hall. Though he says he has heard of the hound since he was in the nursery, he is determined to go to the home of his own people, declaring that no devil in hell and no man on earth can prevent him. Watson believes he was strongly attracted to Miss Stapleton from the first and that the feeling was mutual, and Sir Henry himself says he offered to marry her before her brother interrupted; he also plans changes at the Hall and says he cannot give Selden up, acknowledging that doing so would mean aiding and abetting a felony.

personality.text: Henry Baskerville is a determined man who refuses to be deterred from going to the home of his own people, declaring that no devil or man can stop him (ch 4). He is direct in his dealings, questioning Barrymore at once and in a downright fashion about whether he had received the telegram himself (ch 8). In love he is impulsive, offering in as many words to marry the woman before she could answer (ch 9), yet his feelings are sincere, and the deception he suffered was the saddest part of the affair for him (ch 15). He is also forgiving and fair-minded: he tells Barrymore to forget his harsh words because he cannot blame a man for standing by his wife (ch 9), and he admits that no man could make a more handsome apology than the one who had run at him, despite remembering the look in that man's eyes (ch 9). His compassion shows when he says that, after what has been heard, he cannot bring himself to give the man up (ch 10).

personality.text: Mr. Frankland is defined by a consuming devotion to the law, and he has spent a large fortune in litigation (ch8). His fixations can border on the obsessive: he lies upon the roof of his own house with an excellent telescope, sweeping the moor all day in the hope of glimpsing the escaped convict (ch8). He is also combative and proud of it, boasting that he has established a right of way straight through the centre of old Middleton's park, within a hundred yards of the man's own front door (ch11). Taken together, these details show a man who pursues his disputes and interests with relentless, uncompromising energy.

entities.name: Warning letter
blurbs: Anonymous note on plain foolscap, made of words cut from a Times leading article and pasted with gum, with 'moor' printed in ink: 'As you value your life or your reason keep away from the moor.'

summary.text: The warning letter is an anonymous message examined by Sherlock Holmes in chapter 4. According to the narrator, it was postmarked Charing Cross, posted the preceding evening, and written on a blank half-sheet of paper with no water-mark. Holmes states that its words were assembled from cut-out print, with 'keep away' and 'from the' removed in one piece, and that it was made with nail-scissors. He also states that the word 'moor' was written by hand because it could not be found in print and would be less common. Holmes infers, as his own belief rather than established fact, that the letter was composed by an educated man who wished to pose as an uneducated one. He also observes that the envelope's pen spluttered twice in a word and ran dry three times in a short address, which he takes to show there was very little ink in the bottle.

summary.text: Sir Henry's missing boot, also referred to as the "Meyers, Toronto" boot or the Toronto boot, is a boot taken from Sir Henry Baskerville. In chapter 4 he states that he put both boots outside his door the night before and found only one there in the morning. In chapter 5 he says a black boot was taken the day after a brown one was taken, and the narrator describes a brown boot being drawn from under a cabinet, with someone remarking that there was certainly no boot in it then. In chapter 6 Sir Henry says the other boot is gone for good. In chapter 14 Holmes holds up an old black boot marked "Meyers, Toronto", and his belief, not an established fact, is that it was used to set the hound upon the track. In chapter 15 Holmes states that the first boot procured for him was a new one and therefore useless for his purpose.

summaries.text: Sir Henry's missing boot is an object whose disappearance is reported in chapters 4 and 5. In chapter 4, Sir Henry Baskerville states that he put both of his boots outside his door the previous night and that only one was there in the morning. In chapter 5, Henry Baskerville states that a black boot was taken from him the day after a brown one was taken, so more than one boot has gone missing. Also in chapter 5, the narrator describes a brown boot being drawn from under a cabinet, and someone remarks that there was certainly no boot in it then. The chapters read so far do not say whether this brown boot is the one that was taken, or who took any of the boots.

In chapter 13, Holmes tells Cartwright to send a wire in Holmes's name to Sir Henry Baskerville, saying that if Sir Henry finds the pocketbook Holmes dropped, he is to send it by registered post to Baker Street.

personality.text: Cartwright is portrayed as a diligent and dependable servant. The narrator calls him "my faithful Cartwright" when mentioning that he communicated with him, which marks the trust placed in him (ch 13).

summary.text: Selden is the Notting Hill murderer, a convict whose sentence was commuted over doubts about his sanity, and who escaped from Princetown three days before Perkins reported it in chapter 6. Watson believes that a fortnight later he had not been seen and nothing had been heard of him, but the Barrymores were in fact secretly sustaining him: every second night they put a light in the window to check he was still there, and if there was an answer Barrymore took out bread and meat. When Watson and Sir Henry encounter him on the moor, he screams a curse at them and hurls a rock that splinters against the boulder sheltering them. Watson later states that Selden was wearing Sir Henry's boots, shirt and cap, clothes Barrymore had passed on to help his escape. Sherlock Holmes explains that Selden ran and screamed in terror because he saw the glowing hound on his track.

mention.quote: There is this naturalist, Stapleton, and there is his sister, who is said to be a young lady of attractions.

summary.text: Stapleton, who also appears under the names Jack Stapleton and Vandeleur, is a naturalist living on the moor with a woman he presents as his sister; he says he has been there only two years, arriving shortly after Sir Charles settled. Holmes states that she is in fact his wife, posed as a sister because she would be more useful to him as a free woman, and that Stapleton is the son of Rodger Baskerville, Sir Charles's younger brother, and so truly a Baskerville. According to Holmes, he fled to England under the name Vandeleur after taking public money, ran a school in the east of Yorkshire that came to grief, and is a recognized entomologist; Stapleton himself tells a different story of an epidemic that killed three boys and cost him much of his capital. Holmes states that Stapleton bought the hound in London and kennelled it on the moor, and that he used Mrs. Laura Lyons's letter to lure Sir Charles, while Beryl Stapleton states he kept the hound at an old tin mine on an island in the mire. Holmes believes Stapleton was the bearded man in cab No. 2704 who dogged Holmes and Sir Henry in London, and concludes that he is a Baskerville with designs on the succession, though the false beard is only Holmes's inference. Stapleton is believed to have perished in the Grimpen Mire, since no trace of him reaching the island was found.

summaries.text: Stapleton is a naturalist, according to Sherlock Holmes, who also describes him as having a sister said to be a young lady of attractions. When he meets Watson in chapter 7, Stapleton says he knows who Watson is from the records of Holmes the detective that have reached them, though Watson thinks the tone of his greeting was not altogether cordial. Stapleton states that he has lived on the moor only two years, arriving shortly after Sir Charles settled there, and that he plans to call on Sir Henry that afternoon. By his own account, a serious epidemic broke out in his school, three boys died, and the school never recovered, costing him much of his capital; this is his claim and is not independently confirmed. He also asserts that Sir Charles's nerves were so worked up that the appearance of any dog might have had a fatal effect on his diseased heart, which is likewise Stapleton's opinion rather than established fact.

personality.text: Stapleton is jealously possessive, and his disapproval shows plainly in his face whenever Sir Henry pays attention to his sister (ch 8). He is also a dissembler, able to leave his listeners with the impression that he shares the popular view of an evil influence on families when he does not (ch 8). Above all he is ruthless, determined to have the estate in the end and ready to use any tool or run any risk to get it (ch 15).

summary.text: Beryl Stapleton, also called Miss Stapleton, Mrs. Stapleton, and Beryl Garcia, is a slim, elegant, tall woman, darker than any brunette Watson has seen in England, who contrasts with her light-haired, grey-eyed brother. In chapter 7 she mistakes Watson for Sir Henry and urgently urges him to return to London at once and never set foot on the moor again, adding that her brother would be very angry if he knew she had said anything that might drive Sir Henry away; in chapter 9 Sir Henry reports that she told him the moor was a place of danger and she would never be happy until he left it. In chapter 14 she is described as bearing a whiplash weal across her neck and bruised arms, and she says she realized she had been Stapleton's dupe and tool regarding his love, and that she and Stapleton together planted the wands marking the path through the mire. Holmes states in chapter 15 that she cut out the words forming the message and addressed the letter in a disguised hand, and that threats and even blows could not move her.

Her fear of her brother is evident in her admission that he "would be very angry if he knew that I have said anything which might induce Sir Henry to go away" (ch7). She is also resourceful, cutting out words to form a message and addressing the letter in a disguised hand (ch15). She proves steadfast under coercion, as threats and even blows could not move her (ch15). By the later chapters she is disillusioned, saying she could endure ill-usage, solitude and deception only while she clung to the hope of his love, and that she now knows she has been his dupe and his tool (ch14).

summary.text: Laura Lyons, also called Mrs. Lyons or Mrs. Laura Lyons, lives in Coombe Tracey and is the only person Dr. Mortimer can name with the initials L. L.; he states that she married an artist named Lyons, who came sketching on the moor, proved to be a blackguard and deserted her, and that Stapleton, Sir Charles and Mortimer himself contributed to set her up in a typewriting business. In chapter 11 she admitted writing the letter to Sir Charles, but her account of events is presented as her own claim: she says she never went to the gate because something intervened, that she wanted his help with the expenses of gaining freedom from her husband, and that she got help from another source in the interval. Watson, for his part, senses that she is holding something back despite her coherent story. Holmes later states that she has a close intimacy with Stapleton and, thinking him unmarried, expected to become his wife. In chapter 13 she states that Stapleton dictated the letter to Sir Charles and told her it would hurt his self-respect for another man to find the money, that he had offered her marriage on condition that she divorce her husband, and that he frightened her into remaining silent.

personality.text: Laura Lyons is guarded and evasive when questioned, flatly refusing to discuss her affairs with the words "That is a private matter. I cannot tell it" (ch11).
